title: Begin the Beguine at the University Club for banker Kemper
summary: Harlan Leonard's band sight-read a Latin chart for banker Kemper and Lovett's reading carried it.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: This is what they would bring. I remember once we were on a job and they brought this number, Beguine. "Begin the Begin". You remember that?
Where did this happen, do you remember?
We were playing for one of the biggest

bankers in town, R. Art Crosby Kemper, and they brought this Bequine number "Begin the Begin". This fellow says, "Mr. Kemper wants to hear this number. Can you fellows play it?" Harlan Howlin said, "It's written there isn't it?" "Yes, it's written here".
Oh, they gave you the charts right there?

They gave us the tune. They brought the tune purposely for this and we spread it on out and gave everybody their part and struck right on into it. We didn't play it perfect because we'd never seen it before but we played it. Everybody was pleased with the way we played it and I might say if we'd had a drummer that night that couldn't read music, which Baby Lovett was our drummer, well we never would have made it because it's the latin had rhythm and you've got to read to play it. Everybody had to read his part or else the whole tune would have been a flop, but I had to put that in because -- but down through the years, you know, until a band gets established, you know, you've got a big band, people will try you.

You know, you have people that go along and you know, they -- I mean you had people come up and ask you, you know, "Do you fellows read", you know. Well, you've got a stack of music this high and they're looking at it. Well they, I don't know, are just pessimists or whatever you might call them but
they just -- they don't know much about music or else they could stand off, see, and they could tell whether you were reading your charts or not.
Well tell me, when you were hiring a new man for a band, you gave him the charts and let him read from them to see if he could really read them and read them fast enough?
You would have a rehearsal with him and the rehearsal, you could tell whether he could read or not.

Well, what changes have you seen over the years, Crook, in this thing of reading and playing without charts and anything you can tell us about charts in those days and how they were handled and where you got them?
